# Shepherd of Hermas Chapter 3 — The LOGOS Bible (Formal Equivalent)

**Translator:** LOGOS | **Source:** Codex Sinaiticus (ch 1-31) / P.Mich. 130 (ch 32+), Shepherd of Hermas 3 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-EC/SHE_003_page_001.jpg

---

## Vision 1, Chapter 3

**1** When she had finished speaking with me, she said, "Do you want me to read to you?" "Yes, my lady," I replied. "Then listen and pay attention." She opened the book and read to me things that were magnificent and wonderful, things too great for my memory to contain. For the words were awe-inspiring — more than any person could bear. The final words, however, I retained; for they were within my capacity, and they were gentle: **2** "Behold, the God of Hosts — who by his great power and understanding created the world, and by his glorious counsel clothed his creation with loveliness, and by his mighty word set the heavens in place and founded the earth upon the waters, and by his wise providence and foreknowledge formed his holy church, which he also blessed — behold, he is moving heaven and mountains and hills and seas, and everything is being leveled for his chosen ones, that he may fulfill to them the promise he made with great glory and joy, if they keep the commandments of God which they received in great faith." **3** When she had finished reading and stood up from the chair, four young men came and carried the chair away toward the east. She called me and touched my breast and said to me, "Has my reading pleased you?" I said, "The final words please me, my lady — but the earlier parts were harsh and severe." She replied, "Those final words are for the righteous; but the earlier parts are for the Gentiles and the apostates." **4** While she was talking with me, two men appeared and took her by the arms and carried her away toward the east, where the chair had gone. She departed joyfully, and as she left she said to me, "Be brave, Hermas!"

---

*LOGOS note: "commandments" preferred to "ordinances" for entolai; "Gentiles" better than "heathen" for ethne in early Christian context.*
